{{Elections in Virginia sidebar}}

The '''2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Virginia''' were held on November 8, 2022, to elect the 11 [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representatives]] from the [[U.S. state|state]] of [[Virginia]], one from each of the state's 11 [[Virginia's congressional districts|congressional districts]]. The elections coincided with [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections|other elections]] to the House of Representatives. Pursuant to state law, primaries organized through the Department of Elections were held on June 21, 2022 (the third Tuesday of June). However, some Republican firehouse primaries were held on dates as late as May 21, 2022.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pace|first1=William|title=FIFTH CONGRESSIONAL DISTRICT REPUBLICAN PARTY OFFICIAL 2022 CONVENTION CALL|url=https://virginia5thdistrictgop.files.wordpress.com/2022/01/2022-fifth-district-convention-call-1.pdf|date=February 7, 2022|website=Virginia 5th district GOP|access-date=February 8, 2022|archive-date=June 11, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220611032457/https://virginia5thdistrictgop.files.wordpress.com/2022/01/2022-fifth-district-convention-call-1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Cline|first1=Nathaniel|title=10th Congressional Republicans to select nominee with firehouse primary May 21|url=https://www.loudountimes.com/news/10th-congressional-republicans-to-select-nominee-with-firehouse-primary-may-21/article_70fbe81c-8061-11ec-b9a6-4b1399326ec0.html|date=January 28, 2022|access-date=March 18, 2022|publisher=Loudoun Times-Mirror}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Loposser|first1=Andrew|title=OFFICIAL CALL|url=https://virginia.gop/assets/uploads/2022/02/8thCD-OFFICIAL-Call-V7.pdf|website=Virginia 8th district GOP|access-date=April 17, 2022}}</ref>

== Redistricting ==

===Bipartisan Commission=== 
Following the passage of [[2020 Virginia Question 1|Question 1]] in the [[2020 Virginia elections|2020 elections]], a bipartisan redistricting commission was created. The commission holds 16 members: four from the [[Virginia House of Delegates|House of Delegates]], four from the [[Senate of Virginia]], and eight citizens. It had 60 days following the release of the [[2020 United States census|2020 census]] data or until July 1, 2021, whichever was later, to approve a map, which had to be approved by the [[Virginia General Assembly|General Assembly]].

As the [[2020 United States census|2020 census]] data was released on August 12, 2021<ref>{{Cite web |title=Virginia Redistricting |url=https://www.virginiaredistricting.org/PageReader.aspx?page=News |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=www.virginiaredistricting.org}}</ref> the deadline was set to October 11, 2021. Early in the commission meetings the Democrat and Republican sides both hired partisan map makers and legal advisers. This created worry they would cause the commission to become too partisan to create a compromise map. This was proved true after it became clear that the commission would not create a Congressional map within the deadline after it failed to create any progress on a starting draft for the [[Virginia General Assembly|General Assembly]] maps, which it had solely focused on. The failure of the commission was shown even more clearly when, out of growing frustration from the lack of compromise, three Democratic members of the commission walked out, breaking any chance of a deal.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Moomaw |first=Graham |date=2021-10-08 |title=Va. Redistricting Commission implodes as Republicans reject compromise and Democrats walk out |url=https://www.virginiamercury.com/2021/10/08/va-redistricting-commission-implodes-as-republicans-reject-compromise-and-democrats-walk-out/ |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=Virginia Mercury |language=en-US}}</ref> After the walkout no other progress was made and the deadline passed, handing the redistricting process over to the [[Supreme Court of Virginia|Virginia Supreme Court]].

Following the rules established by Question 1, the court ordered both Democrats and Republicans to create a list of nominees to be selected as [[special master]]s for a map. However, the court threw out 1 of the 3 Republican nominees and ordered a replacement as they found past ties to Republican leadership.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Virginia Supreme Court disqualifies one GOP nominee tapped to redistrict maps |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2021/11/12/virginia-redistricting-gop-special-masters/ |access-date=2023-05-03 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Once the Republican list was re-submitted, the court started reviewing both parties' lists again and picked [[Sean Trende]] as the Republican nominee and [[Bernard Grofman]] as the Democratic nominee.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-19 |title=Virginia Supreme Court appoints two map drawers to help with state's political redistricting |url=https://www.wric.com/news/politics/capitol-connection/virginia-supreme-court-appoints-two-map-drawers-to-help-with-states-political-redistricting/ |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=WRIC ABC 8News |language=en-US}}</ref> On December 8 the two [[special master]]s had announced the completion of the draft map for the [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]].<ref>https://www.vacourts.gov/news/items/2021_1208_scv_press_release_redistricting.pdf Retrieved January 19, 2023.</ref> However, following the announcement it came with public backlash over the handling of incumbents, mostly around the new 7th district. Following the public comment period, the map was almost completely redrawn and a revised map was released on December 28.<ref>https://www.vacourts.gov/courts/scv/districting/redistricting_final.pdf Retrieved January 19, 2023.</ref> The new map's announcement ended the nearly six-month redistricting process.

[[File:Virginia Congressional Districts, 118th Congress.svg|250px|thumb|Virginia's congressional map, 2023–present]]

The new court-approved [[Virginia's congressional districts|map]] completely changed every district, with the largest changes being in the [[Virginia's 1st congressional district|1st]], [[Virginia's 2nd congressional district|2nd]], [[Virginia's 7th congressional district|7th]], and [[Virginia's 10th congressional district|10th]] districts. The first district previously held a significant southern portion of [[Northern Virginia]] and was replaced with the western parts of [[Henrico County, Virginia|Henrico]] and [[Chesterfield County, Virginia|Chesterfield]] counties. These changes made it more Republican.<ref name="FiveThirtyEight Redistrict">{{cite news |title=FiveThirtyEight Redistricting Process, Virginia |url=https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/redistricting-2022-maps/virginia/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210809103936/https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/redistricting-2022-maps/virginia/|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 9, 2021}}</ref> The second district shifted more Republican as it previously held [[Williamsburg, Virginia|Williamsburg City]], [[York County, Virginia|York County]], eastern portions of [[Hampton, Virginia|Hampton City]], and northern parts of [[Norfolk, Virginia|Norfolk City]]. These regions were generally Democratic and were replaced with the southern portions of [[Chesapeake, Virginia|Chesapeake City]], [[Suffolk, Virginia|Suffolk City]], [[Isle of Wight County, Virginia|Isle of Wight County]], [[Franklin, Virginia|Franklin City]], and eastern parts of [[Southampton County, Virginia|Southampton County]], which are generally Republican areas. These changes made it less Republican.<ref name="FiveThirtyEight Redistrict" /> Unlike the 1st and 2nd districts, the new 7th district was entirely remade. The new district now holds the eastern parts of [[Prince William County, Virginia|Prince William County]] and the entirety of [[Culpeper County, Virginia|Culpeper]], [[Madison County, Virginia|Madison]], [[Greene County, Virginia|Greene]], [[Orange County, Virginia|Orange]], [[Stafford County, Virginia|Stafford]], [[King George County, Virginia|King George]], [[Spotsylvania County, Virginia|Spotsylvania]], and [[Caroline County, Virginia|Caroline]] counties. These areas combined are more Democratic than the former Richmond suburbs and rural central Virginia counties which made up the old 7th district.<ref name="FiveThirtyEight Redistrict" /> The last major change district was the 10th district, which removed [[Frederick County, Virginia|Frederick County]], [[Winchester, Virginia|Winchester City]], [[Clarke County, Virginia|Clarke County]], and western parts of [[Fairfax County, Virginia|Fairfax County]]. These were replaced by the addition of western [[Prince William County, Virginia|Prince William County]], [[Fauquier County, Virginia|Fauquier County]], and [[Rappahannock County, Virginia|Rappahannock County]]. This made the district more Republican.<ref name="FiveThirtyEight Redistrict" />

{{see also|Virginia's 1st congressional district}}
The 1st district is based in the western [[Chesapeake Bay]] and includes portions of suburban [[Richmond, Virginia|Richmond]]. Within the district are western [[Henrico County, Virginia|Henrico]] and [[Chesterfield County, Virginia|Chesterfield]] counties. Other localities in the district include [[Colonial Beach, Virginia|Colonial Beach]], [[Mechanicsville, Virginia|Mechanicsville]], and [[Williamsburg, Virginia|Williamsburg]]. The incumbent was Republican [[Rob Wittman]], who was re-elected with 58.2% of the vote in 2020. On November 8, 2022, Congressman Wittman was re-elected.

{{see also|Virginia's 2nd congressional district}}
The 2nd district is based in [[Hampton Roads]], containing the cities of [[Chesapeake, Virginia|Chesapeake]], [[Franklin, Virginia|Franklin]], [[Suffolk, Virginia|Suffolk]], and [[Virginia Beach, Virginia|Virginia Beach]]. Virginia's [[Eastern Shore of Virginia|Eastern Shore]] is also located within the district. The incumbent was Democrat [[Elaine Luria]], who was re-elected with 51.6% of the vote in 2020. Despite her home in [[Norfolk, Virginia|Norfolk]] no longer being in the district, Luria ran for re-election in this seat. On November 8, 2022, State Senator Jen Kiggans won the election to the district, unseating Luria.

{{see also|Virginia's 3rd congressional district}}
The 3rd district encompasses the inner [[Hampton Roads]], including parts of [[Hampton, Virginia|Hampton]] and [[Norfolk, VA|Norfolk]], as well as [[Newport News, VA|Newport News]]. The incumbent was Democrat [[Bobby Scott (politician)|Bobby Scott]], who was reelected with 68.4% of the vote in 2020. On November 8, 2022, Congressman Scott was re-elected.

{{see also|Virginia's 4th congressional district}}
The 4th district takes in the city of [[Richmond, Virginia|Richmond]] and portions of [[Southside (Virginia)|Southside Virginia]] following [[Interstate 95 in Virginia|Interstate 95]]. Within the district are the cities of [[Colonial Heights, Virginia|Colonial Heights]], [[Emporia, Virginia|Emporia]], [[Hopewell, Virginia|Hopewell]], and [[Petersburg, Virginia|Petersburg]]. The incumbent was [[Donald McEachin]], who was re-elected with 61.6% of the vote in 2020.

On November 8, 2022, McEachin was re-elected; however, he died on November 28. A [[2023 Virginia's 4th congressional district special election|special election]] was held on February 21, 2023, with fellow Democrat [[Jennifer McClellan]] elected to succeed him.

{{see also|Virginia's 5th congressional district}}
The 5th district includes the majority of [[Southside (Virginia)|Southside Virginia]]. Within the district are the cities of [[Charlottesville, Virginia|Charlottesville]], [[Danville, Virginia|Danville]], and [[Lynchburg, Virginia|Lynchburg]]. The incumbent representative is [[Bob Good]], who was elected with 52.4% of the vote in 2020, after ousting then Representative [[Denver Riggleman]] in the Republican convention. On November 8, 2022, Congressman Bob Good was re-elected.

{{see also|Virginia's 6th congressional district}}
The 6th district is located in western Virginia taking in the [[Shenandoah Valley]] along [[Interstate 81]]. The district is anchored at the southern end by the cities of [[Roanoke, Virginia|Roanoke]] and [[Salem, Virginia|Salem]]. The incumbent was Republican [[Ben Cline]], who was re-elected with 64.6% of the vote in 2020. On November 8, 2022, Congressman Cline was re-elected.

{{see also|Virginia's 7th congressional district}}
The 7th district is based in [[Northern Virginia|Northern]] and [[Central Virginia]]. The district contains [[Stafford County, Virginia|Stafford]], [[Spotsylvania County, Virginia|Spotsylvania]], [[Greene County, Virginia|Greene]], [[Orange County, Virginia|Orange]], [[Madison County, Virginia|Madison]], [[Culpeper County, Virginia|Culpeper]], [[Caroline County, Virginia|Caroline]], and [[King George County, Virginia|King George]] counties, the city of [[Fredericksburg, Virginia|Fredericksburg]], parts of eastern [[Prince William County, Virginia|Prince William County]], along with a small sliver of [[Albemarle County, Virginia|Albemarle County]]. The incumbent was Democrat [[Abigail Spanberger]], who was re-elected with 50.8% of the vote in 2020. The district was radically redrawn and no longer includes her residence in [[Henrico County, Virginia|Henrico County]]. Despite this, Spanberger ran for re-election in this seat.<ref name="running"/>

The 8th district is based in [[northern Virginia]] and encompasses the inner [[Washington, D.C.]] suburbs, including [[Arlington, Virginia|Arlington]], [[Alexandria, Virginia|Alexandria]], and [[Falls Church, Virginia|Falls Church]]. The incumbent was Democrat [[Don Beyer]], who was re-elected with 75.8% of the vote in 2020. On November 8, 2022, Congressman Beyer was re-elected.

{{see also|Virginia's 9th congressional district}}
The 9th district takes in rural [[southwest Virginia]], including [[Abingdon, Virginia|Abingdon]], [[Blacksburg, Virginia|Blacksburg]], [[Bristol, Virginia|Bristol]] and [[Norton, Virginia|Norton]]. The incumbent was Republican [[Morgan Griffith]], who was re-elected with 94% of the vote in 2020 without opposition from any party. Despite his home in [[Salem, Virginia|Salem]] no longer being in the district. Griffith was running for re-election in this seat.<ref name=VA12-29/> On November 8, 2022, Congressman Morgan Griffith was re-elected.

{{see also|Virginia's 10th congressional district}}
The 10th district is based in northern Virginia and the D.C. metro area, encompassing [[Fauquier County, Virginia|Fauquier]], [[Loudoun County, Virginia|Loudoun]], and [[Rappahannock County, Virginia|Rappahannock]] counties, the independent cities of [[Manassas, Virginia|Mansassas]] and [[Manassas Park, Virginia|Manassas Park]], and portions of [[Fairfax County, Virginia|Fairfax]] and [[Prince William County, Virginia|Prince William]] counties. Democratic incumbent [[Jennifer Wexton]] was re-elected with 56.5% of the vote in 2020.

====Debates and forums====
Both candidates agreed to four joint events.

The first forum was hosted by The Arc of Northern Virginia (NoVA), an advocacy center for disabled children and seniors.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thearcofnova.org/advocacy/|title=NoVA arc advocacy|website=thearcofnova.org}}</ref> They have been hosting these forums since 2020. It was the only online event in which both Wexton and Cao participated. It also included the Democratic and Republican candidates for the 7th and 10th congressional districts. The Arc of NoVA asked their own questions, questions sent to them ahead of time, and questions taken from a Facebook chat. As mentioned at the start of the forum, all candidates were sent the questions they were planning to ask as well as questions that were sent in.

{{see also|Virginia's 11th congressional district}}
The 11th district encompasses portions of suburban [[Washington, D.C.]], including the city of [[Fairfax, Virginia|Fairfax]] and portions of [[Fairfax County, Virginia|Fairfax County]]. The incumbent was Democrat [[Gerry Connolly]], who was re-elected with 71.4% of the vote in 2020. On November 8, 2022, Congressman Connolly was re-elected.
